Where it began

Rudra Pratap Singh, known everywhere as R. P., was born on 6 December 1985 in Raebareli district, in Uttar Pradesh. He first caught the eye with eight wickets at the 2004 Under-19 World Cup, played in Bangladesh, and then kept taking them for Uttar Pradesh in the Ranji Trophy. Away from the nets he studied for a Bachelor of Arts at the University of Lucknow.

His first chance with India came in one-day cricket in 2005. By his third game he already had a match award, for four wickets that kept Sri Lanka to a modest total on a pitch made for batting.

The player

His Test debut, at Faisalabad in January 2006, could hardly have gone better. He took five wickets in the match and was named player of the match. Later, on a tour of England, he took 5 for 59 at Lord's, which remained his best Test return.

The high point came in September 2007, in South Africa, at the World Twenty20. Singh took 12 wickets in seven games, second only to one bowler in the whole event, including 4 for 13 against the hosts in the match that sent them home. India beat Pakistan in the final and took the trophy home. In all he played 14 Tests between 2006 and 2011 and took 40 wickets.

What made him special

He was a left-armer who swung the ball, and he could do it where others found nothing: his early match award against Sri Lanka came on a true batting surface. That gift for movement made him dangerous with the new ball and every bit as useful in the short game.

He would not claim to be an all-rounder. His 116 Test runs came at 7.25, with a best of 30, which is about what you would hope for from a man whose job was to get the other side out.

Away from the middle

He had a fine time in the Indian Premier League. In its second season, in 2009, he was the leading wicket-taker with 23, won the Purple Cap, and saw his side, Deccan Chargers, take the title. He later played for Kochi, Mumbai, Bangalore and Pune, and switched from Uttar Pradesh to Gujarat in 2015. He retired from all cricket in September 2018 and went on to serve as a selector for India's senior men's team.

And finally

In 2006 Leicestershire signed him as an overseas player, then barely saw him: India called him back to the national side and he managed only a handful of games. Counties have lost players to worse causes.
